yt_title: Wafer Sizes: Why 300 mm Matters | From Sand to Wafer Ep 5
yt_description:
Silicon wafers grew from the size of a coin to the size of a dinner plate. Why do chip factories want them bigger, why do most of today's advanced chips come from 300 mm wafers, and why did the jump to 450 mm stall? Pizza maths, edge waste, cost per chip, robots that carry wafers, and what it means for India's first big fab. Simple analogies, no heavy maths.

In this lesson:

slides.head: Wafer Sizes: Why 300 mm Matters
slides.say: You're ordering pizza for a party. Do you buy lots of small pizzas, or a few big ones? Most people pick the big ones. You get more food for your money. Chip factories think the same way about wafers. Last time, we polished wafers into perfect mirrors. Today, we ask a simple question. Why are wafers the size they are? Welcome to episode five of From Sand to Wafer, on Atoms to Chips.

slides.caption: The room on a 300 mm wafer, compared with 200 mm

beats.say: Here's a surprise. A three hundred millimetre wafer is only one and a half times wider than a two hundred millimetre one.
But it has two and a quarter times the room for chips.
Why does that matter to you? It's a big reason the chips in your phone, laptop and car don't cost a fortune.
Let's see how wafers got this big, and why the growing stopped.

slides.head: Wafers keep growing
slides.caption: Every jump meant more chips per wafer

beats.say: In the nineteen sixties, the first wafers were tiny. About one inch across, the size of a coin.

define.meaning: the distance straight across a circle

beats.say: Soon they grew to two inches.
In the seventies came one hundred millimetres, and in the eighties, one hundred and fifty.
Around nineteen ninety, factories moved to two hundred millimetres.
And from around two thousand and one, three hundred millimetres. About the size of a dinner plate. That's still the main size today.
Each jump took about ten years, and each one let factories make many more chips at once.
So why does a little extra width give so much more room? Look at this two hundred millimetre wafer. Twenty centimetres across.
Now the three hundred millimetre wafer. Thirty centimetres. One and a half times wider.
Here's the trick. A wafer grows in two directions at once, wider and taller. Look at these square tiles.

define.meaning: how much flat space a shape covers

beats.say: Two tiles wide gives four tiles. Three tiles wide gives nine. That's more than double.
So one and a half times wider means two and a quarter times the area. Just like a big pizza has far more slices than a small one.
Try it yourself with a ruler. Double the width of a square, and you get four times the space inside.
There's a second win. Chips are square, but wafers are round. Think of cutting square crackers from round dough.
Around the edge, some squares get cut off. Those red pieces can't become working chips.

define.meaning: one chip, cut from the wafer

beats.say: Now take the same big chips, on a three hundred millimetre wafer.
The small wafer fits fifty eight whole chips. The big one fits one hundred and forty eight. More than two and a half times as many.
That's even better than the area alone, because a smaller share of the big wafer is wasted at the edge.

slides.question: A wafer gets 1.5 times wider. How much more area?

beats.say: Quick check. A wafer gets one and a half times wider. How much more area does it have? One and a half times, two and a quarter times, or three times? Pause and think.
Three, two, one.
Two and a quarter times. It grows in both directions, so one and a half times one and a half.

slides.head: Cheaper chips
slides.caption: Each step's cost is shared by more chips

beats.say: Now, money. Making chips takes hundreds of steps. And in most steps, a machine treats one whole wafer in one go.
Think of a washing machine. One load costs about the same, whether it holds three shirts or ten.
A bigger wafer is a fuller load. Each pass through the machine now makes far more chips.
The chemicals, the electricity and the hours in the machine are shared out across all those chips. So each chip carries a smaller slice of the bill.
The machines do cost more, and run a little slower. But the cost of each chip still falls.
When the industry moved to three hundred millimetres, the saving was often put at around thirty percent per chip.

slides.quote: So far: wider wafers hold far more chips, and each chip costs less.
slides.say: So far: wafers grew from coin size to dinner plate size. A little extra width gives a lot more area, less waste at the edge, and cheaper chips. So why not just keep making them bigger?

slides.head: Bigger is harder
slides.caption: Every size jump is a huge engineering job

beats.say: Because bigger is hard. First, weight. A two hundred millimetre wafer weighs about fifty grams. A three hundred millimetre one, about one hundred and thirty.
Second, a wide, thin sheet sags, like a big floppy pizza you hold by the edges.
So three hundred millimetre wafers are made a little thicker, to keep them stiff.
Third, the crystal they're sliced from must be much bigger too. It can weigh hundreds of kilograms, as much as a few people.

define.meaning: the big crystal log wafers are sliced from

beats.say: And fourth, the biggest cost of all. Every machine in the factory must be designed again for the new size.
That's why moving to a new size is a decision for a whole industry, not just one company. Everyone has to move together.
A box of twenty five big wafers is too heavy and too precious for people to carry all day.
So the wafers ride in a sealed plastic box, like a lunchbox that keeps out every speck of dust.

define.meaning: a sealed box that carries wafers around a factory

beats.say: Inside the box, every wafer sits in its own slot, never touching its neighbours. A full box weighs about as much as a big watermelon.
In three hundred millimetre factories, little robot carts carry these boxes along tracks on the ceiling.
They lower each box right onto the machine that needs it. Print, etch, clean, and on to the next.
Like a busy airport baggage system, running day and night.
So is two hundred millimetres finished? Not at all. Think of an old, reliable car that's fully paid for.
Many factories still run two hundred millimetre lines. They make simpler chips, like sensors and power chips for cars and chargers.
Three hundred millimetre factories make the most advanced chips. Phone and laptop processors, and memory.
Both sizes are busy, each doing the job it's best at.

slides.head: What happened to 450 mm?
slides.caption: A bigger wafer that never arrived

beats.say: In the twenty tens, the industry planned the next jump, to four hundred and fifty millimetres. Look how much bigger it is.
Once again, two and a quarter times the area. Big companies even formed a joint research group in New York to test it.
But hundreds of different machines would need to be designed from scratch.
And only a few giant chipmakers could ever afford to buy them. Machine makers couldn't get their money back.
So around twenty sixteen, the effort was put on hold. Three hundred millimetres is still the biggest size in mass production.
One more. Why did four hundred and fifty millimetre wafers stall? Silicon ran out, new machines cost too much, or chips got too big? Pause and think.
Three, two, one.
New machines cost too much. Redesigning a whole factory's worth of tools, for very few buyers, didn't add up.
What about India? Tata Electronics is building the country's first big commercial chip factory, at Dholera in Gujarat.
It's designed for three hundred millimetre wafers, the same size used by the world's leading factories.
As of twenty twenty six, the plan is up to fifty thousand wafers a month when it's fully running.
So the next time you hear about a chip factory, ask one question. What size wafers? Today, the answer that matters most is three hundred millimetres.

slides.head: Today's recap
slides.say: Let's recap. One: wafers grew from coin size to three hundred millimetres. One and a half times wider gives two and a quarter times the area, like a bigger pizza. Two: bigger wafers waste less at the edge, and each machine step is shared by more chips, so every chip costs less. Three: the jump to four hundred and fifty millimetres stalled, because redesigning every machine cost too much. So three hundred millimetres is still king.

slides.say: Some wafers get a special upgrade before any chips are built on them. A fresh, perfect skin of crystal, or a hidden layer of glass inside.
